title: Late Fusion Combines Modality Scores
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Late fusion trains separate unimodal models and combines their predictions or scores at the end.
long: Predict per modality, then combine. It handles missing modalities easily but misses cross-modal interactions.
proof: Each modality produces a score; a weighted combination yields a joint decision.
consequence: A robust baseline for multimodal tasks.

title: Early Fusion Concatenates Modality Features
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Early fusion concatenates features from different modalities before passing them to a joint model.
long: Merge features before making predictions. It allows interactions but requires aligned inputs.
proof: Feature concatenation forms a single joint representation consumed by downstream layers.

title: Spectrograms Represent Time-Frequency Content
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: A spectrogram shows how the frequency content of an audio signal changes over time, usually from a short-time Fourier transform.
short: A picture of sound frequencies over time.
long: A picture of sound frequencies over time. Log-mel spectrograms are common inputs to audio models.
proof: Windowed Fourier transforms produce frequency magnitudes per time frame.
consequence: Allows image-style models to process audio.

title: Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients Compress Speech
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: MFCCs summarize the spectral envelope on a mel scale using a cosine transform of log filter-bank energies.
short: Compact features that mimic human hearing.
long: Compact features that mimic human hearing. They were a standard front end for speech recognition before learned features.
proof: The discrete cosine transform decorrelates log mel energies into a small cepstral vector.

title: Wav2Vec Learns Speech Representations Empirically
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Wav2Vec learns speech representations by contrastive self-supervision over masked audio latents and negative samples, an empirical method.
short: Learn audio features from raw waveform structure.
long: Learn audio features from raw waveform structure. Fine-tuning on transcripts yields strong speech recognition with limited labeled data.
proof: Empirical: contrastive pretraining on unlabeled audio improves downstream recognition accuracy.

title: CTC Loss Aligns Unsegmented Speech to Text
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Connectionist temporal classification sums probability over all monotonic frame-to-label alignments, including blanks, so transcription needs no pre-segmentation.
long: Marginalize over unknown alignments. The blank symbol permits repeated labels and silence.
proof: Forward-backward over the lattice of alignments computes the total probability of collapsing to the target sequence.
consequence: A standard loss for sequence transcription.

title: Whisper Trains on Weakly Supervised Transcripts Empirically
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Empirically, large-scale weakly supervised transcription training yields a speech model that generalizes across languages and tasks.
short: Massive noisy transcripts produce robust speech models.
long: Massive noisy transcripts produce robust speech models. Task prompts let one model perform transcription and translation.
proof: Empirical: training on diverse web-scale audio-text pairs improves robustness on held-out speech benchmarks.
consequence: Highlights the value of scale and diversity in audio data.

title: Text-to-Speech Uses Acoustic Models and Vocoders
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Text-to-speech systems map text to an acoustic representation such as a mel spectrogram and then synthesize a waveform with a vocoder.
short: Predict a spectrogram, then turn it into audio.
long: Predict a spectrogram, then turn it into audio. Modern systems may also generate audio tokens directly.
proof: The acoustic model produces time-frequency features and the vocoder inverts them into samples.
consequence: Separates linguistic content from waveform synthesis.

title: Vision-Language-Action Models Map Pixels to Actions
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Vision-language-action models condition a policy on images and language instructions to output robot actions.
short: One model turns images and words into robot motions.
long: One model turns images and words into robot motions. They are typically fine-tuned from vision-language backbones on robot trajectories.
proof: The observation and instruction are encoded jointly and decoded as an action sequence.
consequence: Shows transfer of web-scale representations to embodied control.

title: Cross-Modal Retrieval Uses Shared Embeddings
subject: Multimodal AI
statement: Cross-modal retrieval maps queries and candidate items from different modalities into a shared space and ranks by embedding similarity.
short: Search images with text using one shared space.
long: Search images with text using one shared space. The same machinery supports text-to-image and image-to-text search.
proof: Joint training aligns encoders so that paired items have high similarity.
consequence: Underpins multilingual and multimodal search interfaces.

title: Typographic Attacks Mislead Vision-Language Models Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Empirically, placing misleading text inside an image can flip a vision-language model's classification toward the written word.
short: Words printed in an image can fool the model.
long: Words printed in an image can fool the model. This reveals heavy reliance on linguistic features in visual encoders.
proof: Empirical: adding a text label to an object image changes predicted class in controlled experiments.
consequence: A concrete robustness failure of multimodal systems.

title: Partially Observable MDP Has Hidden State
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: A partially observable Markov decision process extends an MDP by giving the agent observations generated from a hidden state rather than the state itself.
short: The agent sees observations, not the true state.
long: The agent sees observations, not the true state. Policies may keep belief states or recurrent memory.
proof: The transition and observation models define a belief update over hidden states.
consequence: Models realistic robotics and planning under uncertainty.

title: Model Predictive Control Replans Each Step
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Model predictive control solves a finite-horizon optimal-control problem at each step, applies the first action and replans with new observations.
short: Plan briefly, act once, then replan.
long: Plan briefly, act once, then replan. Receding-horizon replanning corrects model errors.
proof: At each time a fresh optimization uses the current state estimate and discards the rest of the old plan.
consequence: A standard robust control strategy in robotics.

title: Imitation Learning Clones Expert Actions
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Behavioral cloning learns a policy by supervised regression from expert state-action demonstrations.
short: Learn to copy the expert's actions.
long: Learn to copy the expert's actions. It needs no reward function but depends on demonstration coverage.
proof: The expert action is treated as a supervised label for each demonstrated state.
consequence: A simple way to bootstrap policies from data.

title: Behavioral Cloning Suffers Covariate Shift
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Small cloning errors move the agent off the demonstration distribution, where further errors grow and compound.
short: One small mistake leads to unfamiliar states.
long: One small mistake leads to unfamiliar states. This is why cloned policies can fail despite low held-out action error.
proof: A wrong action changes the next state, which may lie outside the support of demonstrations.
consequence: Motivates data aggregation and on-policy correction methods.

title: DAgger Aggregates Expert Corrections
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Dataset aggregation iteratively runs the current policy, asks an expert to label visited states and retrains on the growing dataset.
short: Collect expert corrections on the states the learner visits.
long: Collect expert corrections on the states the learner visits. This addresses the covariate shift of behavioral cloning.
proof: Adding expert labels for learner-induced states makes the training distribution match the deployment distribution.
consequence: Improves imitation stability in sequential tasks.

title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning Infers Rewards
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks a reward function under which observed expert behavior is near-optimal.
short: Infer what goal explains the demonstrations.
long: Infer what goal explains the demonstrations. The inferred reward can generalize to new situations.
proof: Optimality conditions link behavior to rewards, so demonstration likelihood can score candidate rewards.
consequence: Bases preferences on goals rather than copied actions.

title: Domain Randomization Aids Sim-to-Real Transfer Empirically
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Domain randomization varies simulator parameters widely during training so that real-world dynamics appear as one sample from the training distribution, an empirical technique.
short: Train on many simulated worlds to handle the real one.
long: Train on many simulated worlds to handle the real one. Randomized visuals and physics encourage robust policies.
proof: Empirical: policies trained with wide parameter variation transfer better to real robots than single-environment training.
consequence: Reduces the reality gap in robotics.

title: Offline RL Learns from Fixed Datasets
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from a fixed logged dataset without further interaction with the environment.
long: Learn from logged experience only. Extrapolation errors on unseen actions are the main challenge.
proof: The dataset replaces online rollouts as the source of transitions.
consequence: Makes RL applicable where exploration is costly or unsafe.

title: Conservative Q-Learning Penalizes OOD Actions
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: Conservative Q-learning adds a penalty that lowers Q-values for actions not present in the offline dataset, reducing extrapolation error.
short: Keep Q-values low for unfamiliar actions.
long: Keep Q-values low for unfamiliar actions. This discourages the policy from exploiting erroneous high estimates.
proof: The penalty subtracts expected Q on dataset actions from a log-sum-exp over all actions.
consequence: A standard baseline for offline RL.

title: Safety Shields Filter Unsafe Actions
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: A safety shield monitors proposed actions and replaces those that violate a formal safety specification with safe alternatives.
short: A runtime filter blocks dangerous actions.
long: A runtime filter blocks dangerous actions. Shields can be synthesized from temporal-logic constraints.
proof: The checker evaluates the action against the specification before execution.
consequence: Gives formal safety guarantees at runtime.

title: Occupancy Grids Represent Free Space
subject: Reinforcement Learning
statement: An occupancy grid discretizes the environment into cells marked free, occupied or unknown for robot planning.
short: A map of which cells are blocked.
long: A map of which cells are blocked. Sensor readings update cell probabilities over time.
proof: Discretizing space and fusing measurements yields a per-cell occupancy estimate.
consequence: A basic representation for mobile-robot navigation.

title: Structural Causal Model Encodes Interventions
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: A structural causal model consists of exogenous noise variables and structural equations that define each variable as a function of its parents and noise.
short: Variables are generated by explicit mechanisms.
long: Variables are generated by explicit mechanisms. An intervention replaces one structural equation with a fixed value.
proof: The equations define the observational distribution and, after replacement, interventional distributions.
consequence: Provides a formal language for causality.

title: do-Calculus Identifies Interventional Distributions
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Do-calculus gives three rules for transforming probabilities with interventions into expressions involving only observational distributions when graphical conditions hold.
short: Rewrite interventions as observations when possible.
long: Rewrite interventions as observations when possible. Identification fails when confounding cannot be blocked.
proof: The rules follow from the invariance of mechanisms under interventions in a causal DAG.
consequence: Foundation of causal inference from observational data.

title: Backdoor Criterion Blocks Spurious Paths
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: The backdoor criterion identifies a set of covariates whose adjustment removes confounding between treatment and outcome in a causal graph.
short: Adjust for variables that close backdoor paths.
long: Adjust for variables that close backdoor paths. Adjusting for colliders can instead create bias.
proof: Conditioning on a valid backdoor set blocks every noncausal path from treatment to outcome.
consequence: Justifies covariate adjustment in observational studies.

title: Frontdoor Criterion Identifies Effects
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: The frontdoor criterion identifies a causal effect through an observed mediator even when treatment and outcome share unobserved confounding.
short: Use a mediator to bypass hidden confounding.
long: Use a mediator to bypass hidden confounding. It requires the mediator to intercept all causal paths and be unconfounded with the outcome given treatment.
proof: The identification formula chains the treatment-to-mediator and mediator-to-outcome effects.
consequence: Enables identification in some otherwise intractable settings.

title: Instrumental Variables Handle Unobserved Confounding
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: An instrumental variable affects the outcome only through the treatment, allowing identification despite unobserved treatment-outcome confounding.
short: Use an external nudge to isolate causal effect.
long: Use an external nudge to isolate causal effect. Validity requires relevance, independence and exclusion restrictions.
proof: The instrument shifts treatment without directly changing the outcome, so its association with the outcome scales with the causal effect.
consequence: A central tool in econometrics and causal ML.

title: Difference-in-Differences Removes Time-Invariant Bias
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Difference-in-differences estimates a treatment effect by comparing pre-to-post changes in treated and untreated groups.
long: Compare changes, not just levels. It relies on parallel trends in the absence of treatment.
proof: Time-invariant group differences cancel in the double difference.
consequence: Widely used for policy and observational effect estimation.

title: Propensity Score Matching Balances Covariates
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Propensity score matching pairs treated and control units with similar probabilities of treatment given covariates to reduce confounding.
short: Match people with similar treatment chances.
long: Match people with similar treatment chances. Balance diagnostics check whether matching succeeded.
proof: Conditional on the propensity score, treatment is independent of covariates under ignorability.

title: Double Machine Learning Debiases Treatment Effects
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Double machine learning uses cross-fitted nuisance estimates and orthogonal scores so that regularization errors do not bias the treatment-effect estimate.
short: Cross-fit nuisances to remove first-order bias.
long: Cross-fit nuisances to remove first-order bias. Neyman orthogonality makes the estimator robust to slow nuisance learning.
proof: Cross-fitting independentizes nuisance estimates from the evaluation sample and orthogonality cancels first-order errors.
consequence: Brings flexible ML into valid causal inference.

title: Causal Forests Estimate Heterogeneous Effects
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Causal forests use tree ensembles with honest splitting to estimate how treatment effects vary across covariates.
short: Trees that estimate local treatment effects.
long: Trees that estimate local treatment effects. Honest splitting uses separate data for tree structure and effect estimation.
proof: Local randomized or residualized comparisons are averaged over trees to produce conditional effect estimates.

title: Invariant Risk Minimization Seeks Stable Predictors
subject: Machine Learning Theory
statement: Invariant risk minimization aims to learn representations whose optimal classifier is the same across training environments, encouraging out-of-distribution generalization.
short: Seek features that work the same in every environment.
long: Seek features that work the same in every environment. The penalty encourages the invariance of the optimal linear predictor.
proof: Requiring a shared optimal classifier across environments discourages reliance on environment-specific correlations.
consequence: A theoretical approach to causal feature learning.

title: Invariant Risk Minimization Can Fail Empirically
subject: Machine Learning Theory
statement: Empirically, invariant risk minimization can fail on nonlinear or insufficiently varied environments, sometimes learning degenerate invariant solutions.
short: Invariance penalties do not always deliver robustness.
long: Invariance penalties do not always deliver robustness. Careful environment design and diagnostics matter.
proof: Empirical: constructed nonlinear tasks show IRM converging to trivial constant classifiers.
consequence: Highlights gaps between invariance theory and practice.

title: Truncated Factorization Gives Interventional Distributions
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: In a causal Bayesian network, the distribution after intervening on a set of variables factors with the structural equations for the intervened variables replaced by point masses.
latex: P(y\mid do(x))=\prod_{i\notin X}P(x_i\mid x_{\mathrm{pa}(i)})\ \mathbf{1}[x_i=\hat{x}_i\ \mathrm{for}\ i\in X]
short: Cut incoming edges for intervened nodes.
long: Cut incoming edges for intervened nodes. This is the truncated factorization formula.
proof: The intervention removes the parents of each manipulated variable, so those factors vanish from the joint.
consequence: Connects graph structure to intervention calculations.

title: Counterfactual Fairness Requires a Causal Model
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Counterfactual fairness requires a decision to be unchanged in a counterfactual world where only the protected attribute is altered, which needs a causal model to define.
short: Fairness can be defined by counterfactual invariance.
long: Fairness can be defined by counterfactual invariance. Without causal assumptions the counterfactual is not identifiable.
proof: Changing a protected attribute while holding other variables fixed requires specifying which descendants change.
consequence: Makes causal assumptions explicit in fairness analysis.

title: Collider Conditioning Can Reverse Associations
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Conditioning on a common effect of two variables can create a spurious association between them, potentially reversing the sign of an estimated effect.
latex: X\perp Y,\ \mathrm{but}\ X\not\perp Y\mid C,\ C\leftarrow X,\ C\leftarrow Y
short: Selecting on a common effect creates false dependence.
long: Selecting on a common effect creates false dependence. This is Berkson's paradox or collider bias.
proof: Conditioning on a collider opens a path between its parents in the graphical criterion.

title: Federated Averaging Aggregates Local Updates
subject: Machine Learning
statement: Federated averaging trains locally on each client for several steps and averages the resulting model updates on a server.
long: Train locally, average globally. Weighting by client sample size is the standard aggregation rule.
proof: Local SGD steps approximate a global step; averaging combines the clients' estimates.
consequence: The foundational algorithm of federated learning.

title: Federated Rounds Dominate Communication Cost
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: In federated learning the bottleneck is often the repeated exchange of model updates between server and clients, not local computation.
short: Sending models costs more than training locally.
long: Sending models costs more than training locally. Compression and fewer local steps trade accuracy for less communication.
proof: Each round transmits a full model to selected clients and back, which dominates when models are large.
consequence: Drives research on communication-efficient federated algorithms.

title: Non-IID Clients Slow Federated Convergence Empirically
subject: Machine Learning
statement: Empirically, heterogeneous client data distributions make local updates diverge and slow or destabilize federated convergence.
short: Different clients pull the model in different directions.
long: Different clients pull the model in different directions. Personalization and proximal terms mitigate client drift.
proof: Empirical: non-IID partitions produce lower accuracy and more client drift than shuffled IID partitions.
consequence: Client heterogeneity is a central federated challenge.

title: Secure Aggregation Hides Individual Updates
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Secure aggregation protocols let a server recover only the sum of client updates without seeing any individual update.
short: The server sees only the aggregate.
long: The server sees only the aggregate. Pairwise masks cancel when updates are summed.
proof: Cryptographic masks are chosen so that each client's mask cancels with others in the aggregate.
consequence: Reduces privacy leakage from update inspection.

title: DP-SGD Clips Gradients and Adds Noise
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Differentially private SGD clips each example's gradient to a fixed norm and adds calibrated Gaussian noise to the averaged gradient.
short: Clip per-example influence, then add noise.
long: Clip per-example influence, then add noise. Privacy accounting tracks the budget across training steps.
proof: Bounding sensitivity by C and adding noise proportional to C gives differential privacy by the Gaussian mechanism.

title: Privacy Loss Composes Across Queries
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Under sequential composition, the privacy parameters of multiple mechanisms applied to the same data add.
short: Each query spends part of the privacy budget.
long: Each query spends part of the privacy budget. Advanced composition can give tighter bounds for many queries.
proof: The failure probability of a chain of private mechanisms is bounded by the sum of individual bounds.
consequence: Requires budget accounting for long training runs.

title: Renyi Differential Privacy Simplifies Accounting
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Renyi differential privacy measures privacy loss with Renyi divergences and offers tight composition for repeated Gaussian mechanisms.
short: A divergence-based budget that composes cleanly.
long: A divergence-based budget that composes cleanly. It can be converted back to standard differential privacy guarantees.
proof: Renyi divergences compose additively under product mechanisms, simplifying the analysis of many steps.
consequence: Underlies modern privacy accounting for DP-SGD.

title: Membership Inference Exploits Confidence Gaps
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Membership inference attacks guess whether a record was in training by exploiting higher confidence or lower loss on memorized examples.
short: Trained-on examples often look more familiar.
long: Trained-on examples often look more familiar. Calibration and regularization can reduce the signal.
proof: Empirical: members have systematically lower loss than comparable nonmembers.
consequence: Reveals privacy leakage from model outputs.

title: Model Inversion Reconstructs Class Representatives
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Model inversion attacks optimize an input to maximize a model's confidence for a target class, recovering class-representative data.
short: Optimize an input that looks like a target class.
long: Optimize an input that looks like a target class. Successful reconstruction leaks information about training classes.
proof: Gradient ascent on class probability produces inputs resembling the learned class prototype.
consequence: Shows privacy risk from exposed model predictions.

title: Training Data Can Be Extracted from Language Models Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Empirically, language models can be made to reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, including sensitive text.
short: Models sometimes recite their training data.
long: Models sometimes recite their training data. Extraction attacks use tailored prompts and likelihood searches.
proof: Empirical: extraction studies recover memorized documents from deployed language models.
consequence: Motivates data sanitization and privacy-preserving training.

title: Homomorphic Encryption Allows Computing on Ciphertexts
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Homomorphic encryption supports computing a function on encrypted data so that decrypting the result matches computing the function on plaintext.
long: Compute without decrypting the data. Fully homomorphic schemes support arbitrary circuits with bootstrapping.
proof: The encryption scheme provides operations whose ciphertext results decrypt to the corresponding plaintext operations.
consequence: Enables privacy-preserving inference on untrusted servers.

title: Federated Learning Trades Accuracy for Privacy Empirically
subject: Machine Learning
statement: Empirically, adding differential privacy to federated training lowers utility, with stronger privacy budgets causing larger accuracy losses.
long: Stronger privacy usually costs accuracy. The trade-off depends on model size, client count and clipping settings.
proof: Empirical: federated experiments sweep the privacy budget and observe monotone accuracy changes.

title: Watermarks Embed Statistical Signals in Generations
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: A watermark deliberately biases generated output so that a statistical test can later identify it as model-generated.
short: Hide a detectable signature in the output.
long: Hide a detectable signature in the output. Watermarks may modify tokens, images or continuous signals.
proof: The embedding rule changes the output distribution in a known way that a detector tests for.

title: Green List Watermarks Bias Token Sampling
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Token-level watermarking partitions the vocabulary into a green list and red list based on prior tokens and slightly favors green-list sampling.
short: Nudge sampling toward a key-dependent word list.
long: Nudge sampling toward a key-dependent word list. The key determines the partition, so unauthorized parties cannot forge the pattern.
proof: Biasing logits by a constant delta raises green-list probability while keeping sampling nearly lossless.
consequence: A practical watermark for language-model output.

title: Watermark Detection Uses Statistical Tests
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: A watermark detector counts green-list tokens and tests whether the count exceeds what chance sampling would produce.
short: Count signature tokens and compute a z-score.
long: Count signature tokens and compute a z-score. Longer texts give higher detection power.
proof: Under the null, green-list counts follow a binomial distribution with probability equal to the green-list fraction.
consequence: Gives a principled false-positive rate for detection.

title: Watermarks Degrade under Paraphrasing Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, paraphrasing or heavy editing can remove statistical watermarks from generated text.
short: Rewriting can wash out the signature.
long: Rewriting can wash out the signature. Robust watermarks are an active area of research.
proof: Empirical: detector scores drop after paraphrasing attacks while text meaning is preserved.
consequence: Limits watermark reliability in adversarial settings.

title: AI-Text Detectors Generalize Poorly Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, AI-generated-text detectors trained on one model or domain often fail on unseen generators and domains.
short: Detectors overfit to the generator they saw.
long: Detectors overfit to the generator they saw. Performance also drops on edited or translated text.
proof: Empirical: cross-model and cross-domain evaluations show large accuracy drops.
consequence: Detectors should not be treated as definitive evidence.

title: Detector False Positives Affect Nonnative Writers Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, AI-text detectors flag non-native writing at higher rates than native writing, raising fairness concerns.
short: Detectors can wrongly accuse non-native writers.
long: Detectors can wrongly accuse non-native writers. Stylistic differences overlap with learned machine-text features.
proof: Empirical: controlled studies report elevated false-positive rates for non-native English essays.
consequence: Discourages punitive use of automatic detectors.

title: C2PA Metadata Records Content Provenance
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: C2PA is an open standard for cryptographically signed provenance metadata that records how media was created or edited.
short: Signed metadata tracks where media came from.
long: Signed metadata tracks where media came from. The chain of assertions can record generative-model involvement.
proof: The standard defines signed manifests verifiable against the content hash.
consequence: Supports content credentials rather than post hoc detection.

title: Predictive Entropy Splits into Two Uncertainties
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: For a Bayesian predictive distribution, mutual information between parameters and labels separates epistemic uncertainty from expected aleatoric entropy.
short: Total uncertainty equals data noise plus model uncertainty.
long: Total uncertainty equals data noise plus model uncertainty. The two terms are often called aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty.
proof: Expand the entropy of the posterior predictive distribution by the chain rule for entropy.
consequence: Guides uncertainty-aware decision making and active learning.

title: Deep Ensembles Estimate Epistemic Uncertainty
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: A deep ensemble averages several independently trained networks and uses disagreement among their predictions as an epistemic-uncertainty estimate.
short: Several models disagree when they are unsure.
long: Several models disagree when they are unsure. Ensembles empirically improve calibration as well as accuracy.
proof: Different random initializations and data orders yield functionally diverse predictors whose spread reflects model uncertainty.

title: Monte Carlo Dropout Approximates Posterior Uncertainty
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Keeping dropout active at inference and averaging stochastic forward passes approximates Bayesian inference over network weights.
short: Sample dropout masks to get uncertainty.
long: Sample dropout masks to get uncertainty. It is cheap but often less calibrated than deep ensembles.
proof: Dropout corresponds to a variational distribution over weights, so stochastic passes sample from that approximate posterior.
consequence: A low-cost uncertainty estimate for neural networks.

title: Conformal Prediction Gives Marginal Coverage
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Conformal prediction constructs prediction sets whose marginal coverage is at least a target level under exchangeability, without assuming a model form.
long: Guaranteed average coverage under exchangeability. The guarantee is distribution-free but marginal over future samples.
proof: Exchangeability makes the new conformity score rank uniformly among calibration scores.

title: Split Conformal Uses a Calibration Holdout
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Split conformal prediction fits a model on a training set and computes a conformity-score quantile on a separate calibration set.
short: Calibrate prediction-set size on held-out scores.
long: Calibrate prediction-set size on held-out scores. It avoids refitting the model for each calibration point.
proof: The held-out scores are exchangeable with the future score, so their empirical quantile gives valid coverage.
consequence: Makes conformal prediction cheap for large models.

title: Conformal Coverage Is Marginal Not Conditional
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Standard conformal guarantees hold on average over draws, not necessarily for each subgroup or each feature value.
short: Average coverage does not promise per-group coverage.
long: Average coverage does not promise per-group coverage. Conditional or group-conditional conformal methods address this gap.
proof: The exchangeability argument applies to the pooled distribution, not to arbitrary conditional slices.
consequence: Requires subgroup audits for high-stakes use.

title: Post-hoc Calibration Depends on the Calibration Set
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Post-hoc calibration methods such as temperature scaling estimate their parameters from a held-out set, so their quality depends on its size and distribution.
short: A calibrator is only as good as its calibration data.
long: A calibrator is only as good as its calibration data. Mismatch between calibration and deployment distributions degrades reliability.
proof: The fitted temperature minimizes a proper score on the calibration set.
consequence: Requires fresh calibration under distribution change.

title: Maximum Calibration Error Bounds Worst-Bin Gap
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Maximum calibration error is the largest absolute difference between confidence and empirical accuracy over confidence bins.
long: The worst bin's confidence-accuracy gap. It is more sensitive to rare bins than expected calibration error.
proof: Partition predictions by confidence, compute accuracy per bin and take the maximum deviation.
consequence: Useful when failures must be bounded in every region.

title: Brier Score Measures Probabilistic Accuracy
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: The Brier score is the mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and binary outcomes, rewarding both discrimination and calibration.
long: Squared error on predicted probabilities. Lower is better, with zero for perfect forecasts.
proof: It is the mean squared error of probability forecasts against binary outcomes.
consequence: A standard score for probabilistic classifiers.

title: Log Loss Is a Proper Scoring Rule
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: The logarithmic scoring rule is proper: its expected value is minimized when reported probabilities equal the true probabilities.
short: Honest probabilities minimize expected log loss.
long: Honest probabilities minimize expected log loss. The difference in expected scores is a KL divergence.
proof: Subtracting expected score at the true distribution gives KL(q,p), which is nonnegative.
consequence: Justifies cross-entropy as a training objective.

title: Proper Scoring Rules Reward Honest Probabilities
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: For a proper scoring rule, reporting a distribution other than one's true belief cannot lower the expected score.
short: Truthful forecasts are optimal under proper scores.
long: Truthful forecasts are optimal under proper scores. Brier score and log loss are both proper; accuracy is not.
proof: Properness is exactly the inequality that the expected score is maximized at the true distribution.
consequence: Explains why probabilistic training objectives encourage calibrated predictions.

title: Distance-Based Out-of-Distribution Detection
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: A simple OOD detector flags inputs whose representation is far from the nearest training examples or far from the training centroid.
short: Unfamiliar inputs look far from training data.
long: Unfamiliar inputs look far from training data. Mahalanobis distance and nearest-neighbour distance are common variants.
proof: Under the assumption that in-distribution features form compact clusters, distance acts as a novelty score.
consequence: A widely used baseline for open-world recognition.

title: Open-Set Recognition Rejects Unknown Classes
subject: Computer Vision
statement: Open-set recognition requires a classifier to assign known labels to known classes and reject inputs from classes unseen during training.
short: Classifiers should be able to say I do not know.
long: Classifiers should be able to say I do not know. This differs from closed-set evaluation where every test class is known.
proof: The decision rule includes an additional reject option based on confidence or distance.
consequence: Important for deployment in uncontrolled environments.

title: Covariate Shift Correction by Importance Weighting
subject: Machine Learning Theory
statement: When only the input distribution changes and the conditional label distribution stays fixed, reweighting training examples by the density ratio yields an unbiased target risk.
short: Reweight source samples to match the target inputs.
long: Reweight source samples to match the target inputs. Density-ratio estimation is the practical difficulty.
proof: Changing the integration measure from source to target introduces the density ratio as a weight.
consequence: A principled approach to covariate shift adaptation.

title: Distributionally Robust Optimization Minimizes Worst-Case Risk
subject: Machine Learning Theory
statement: Distributionally robust optimization minimizes the worst expected loss over an ambiguity set of plausible distributions near the empirical one.
short: Optimize against the worst plausible distribution.
long: Optimize against the worst plausible distribution. The ambiguity set may be defined by a divergence ball or moments.
proof: The minimax objective replaces a single empirical distribution with a set of alternatives.

title: Integrated Gradients Accumulate Path Attributions
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Integrated gradients attributes a prediction to input features by integrating the gradient along a path from a baseline to the input.
short: Accumulate gradients along a baseline-to-input path.
long: Accumulate gradients along a baseline-to-input path. It satisfies completeness: attributions sum to the output difference.
proof: The fundamental theorem of calculus recovers the output change by integrating directional derivatives.
consequence: A widely used gradient-based explanation method.

title: Occlusion Sensitivity Measures Prediction Drops
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Occlusion sensitivity perturbs or masks input regions and measures the drop in prediction confidence to estimate their importance.
short: Hide a region and see how much the score falls.
long: Hide a region and see how much the score falls. It is model-agnostic but can be slow for many regions.
proof: The change in output after masking defines a direct importance score for the region.
consequence: A simple interpretability baseline for vision models.

title: Concept Bottleneck Models Predict Concepts First
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: A concept bottleneck model first predicts human-defined concepts and then predicts the final label from those concepts.
short: Predict understandable concepts before the answer.
long: Predict understandable concepts before the answer. Concept-level interventions allow testing what the model believes.
proof: Training uses concept labels, and the final layer depends only on predicted concepts.
consequence: Improves interpretability by exposing intermediate concepts.

title: Counterfactual Explanations Find Minimal Changes
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: A counterfactual explanation finds a nearby input that changes the model's decision, describing what would have to change for a different outcome.
short: Show the smallest edit that flips the decision.
long: Show the smallest edit that flips the decision. Feasibility constraints keep counterfactuals realistic.
proof: Optimize a distance to the original input subject to the model changing its prediction.

title: Attention Is Not Sufficient Explanation
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Attention weights alone do not reliably explain a model's prediction: different parameter settings can yield the same output with different attention patterns.
short: High attention does not prove causal importance.
long: High attention does not prove causal importance. Ablation studies often contradict attention-based explanations.
proof: Empirical: constructed models produce identical predictions while attention weights vary.
consequence: Requires causal tests instead of reading weights directly.

title: Faithfulness and Plausibility of Explanations Differ
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: An explanation can be plausible to humans while being unfaithful to the model's actual computation, and vice versa.
long: Convincing explanations can be wrong. Evaluation should test both human understandability and causal fidelity.
proof: Empirical: post hoc explanations change under parameter perturbations without matching changes in prediction.
consequence: Highlights a gap in explainability evaluation.

title: Anchors Give High-Precision Local Rules
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Anchors explain individual predictions with simple if-then rules whose conditions guarantee the prediction with high probability for perturbed inputs.
short: Find rules that almost always lock in the prediction.
long: Find rules that almost always lock in the prediction. Reinforcement-learning search builds rules by adding conditions.
proof: The rule is validated by sampling perturbations and requiring high prediction stability.

title: Test Loss Follows a Power Law in Data Empirically
subject: Machine Learning Theory
statement: Empirical scaling studies find test loss decays approximately as a power law in dataset size over several orders of magnitude.
short: More data yields predictably diminishing losses.
long: More data yields predictably diminishing losses. Extrapolation beyond observed ranges is uncertain.
proof: Empirical: fitted log-log curves for held-out loss are approximately linear across dataset sizes.

title: Chinchilla Token Budget Is Empirical
subject: Machine Learning Theory
statement: Empirical compute-optimal scaling found that for a fixed compute budget many large language models were undertrained relative to their parameter count.
short: More tokens per parameter than earlier rules suggested.
long: More tokens per parameter than earlier rules suggested. The result comes from trained model families, not from a theorem.
proof: Empirical: isoFLOP comparisons show lower loss when parameters and tokens are scaled together.
consequence: Changed how training budgets are allocated.

title: Emergent Abilities May Be a Metric Artifact
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirical analyses suggest that apparently abrupt emergence of capabilities can arise from smooth metrics such as accuracy or cross-entropy viewed on discontinuous scales.
short: Sharp emergence may be a scoring illusion.
long: Sharp emergence may be a scoring illusion. The debate concerns measurement, not whether capabilities improve.
proof: Empirical: replacing pass-or-fail metrics with continuous ones makes many jumps look gradual.
consequence: Calls for caution in claims about phase transitions.

title: In-Context Learning Resembles Bayesian Inference
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Empirical and theoretical work connects in-context learning to implicit Bayesian inference over tasks suggested by the prompt examples.
short: Prompts can act like evidence about the task.
long: Prompts can act like evidence about the task. Alternative accounts emphasize induction circuits and template matching.
proof: Constructed tasks show predictions consistent with posterior inference over latent concepts.
consequence: Provides a conceptual framework for prompting.

title: Few-Shot Label Distribution Biases Predictions Empirically
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Empirically, the distribution of labels in few-shot demonstrations biases the model's predicted label distribution.
long: Demonstration labels skew the answers. Balanced demonstration sets reduce the skew.
proof: Empirical: varying demo label frequencies shifts prediction frequencies on the same queries.

title: Chain-of-Thought Emerges with Scale Empirically
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Empirically, prompting for intermediate reasoning steps improves performance mainly for sufficiently large models.
short: Step-by-step prompting pays off at scale.
long: Step-by-step prompting pays off at scale. Small models can even be hurt by such prompts.
proof: Empirical: scaling studies compare direct and chain-of-thought prompts across model sizes.
consequence: Links reasoning behavior to model scale.

title: Self-Consistency Averages Reasoning Paths
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Self-consistency samples multiple reasoning chains and selects the most frequent final answer instead of relying on a single chain.
long: Vote across many reasoning paths. It trades inference cost for reliability.
proof: Sampling diverse chains lets consistent answers accumulate support across independent derivations.

title: Least-to-Most Prompting Decomposes Problems
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Least-to-most prompting first decomposes a problem into subproblems and then solves them in order, using earlier answers as context.
short: Break a hard problem into easier steps.
long: Break a hard problem into easier steps. It helps on compositional tasks such as multi-hop reasoning.
proof: Solving simpler subquestions first supplies intermediate results needed for later steps.
consequence: A structured alternative to single-pass reasoning.

title: Tree of Thoughts Explores Reasoning Branches
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Tree-of-thought prompting maintains several partial reasoning paths, evaluates them and expands the most promising ones.
long: Search over several reasoning branches. It borrows from search algorithms rather than following one chain.
proof: Generating and scoring candidate continuations lets the system prune weak paths.
consequence: Improves planning on tasks with multiple solution routes.

title: Instruction Tuning Improves Zero-Shot Behavior Empirically
subject: Natural Language Processing
statement: Empirically, fine-tuning language models on diverse instruction-response pairs improves their zero-shot performance on unseen tasks.
short: Training on instructions helps on new instructions.
long: Training on instructions helps on new instructions. Data diversity matters more than sheer volume in many studies.
proof: Empirical: instruction-tuned models outperform their base versions on held-out task formats.
consequence: A standard step in building general-purpose assistants.
